cues.text: In July of AD 64, a catastrophic fire tore through Rome , destroying much of the city over the course of six days.

Rumor quickly spread that Emperor Nero himself had ordered the blaze, whether to clear space for his own architectural ambitions or from simple indifference to the suffering it caused — the enduring image of Nero 'fiddling while Rome burned,' though likely more legend than fact, reflects the depth of public suspicion that fell on him.
Alarmed by the growing popular anger directed at him, Nero moved to deflect blame onto the small, poorly understood Christian community already present in the city.

The Roman historian Tacitus , no friend to Christianity himself, records that Nero 'punished with the utmost refinements of cruelty a class hated for their abominations, called Christians' — direct outside confirmation, from a hostile pagan source, of the persecution's basic facts.

According to Tacitus's account, the condemned Christians were killed in deliberately theatrical and horrifying ways: some were sewn into the skins of wild animals and torn apart by dogs in the public arena, others were crucified, and still others were coated in pitch and set alight as living torches to illuminate Nero's own gardens after dark, providing grim entertainment for an evening spectacle.
This same Neronian persecution is traditionally understood to have claimed the lives of Sts.
Peter and Paul , whose own feast on 29 June immediately precedes this memorial in the Church's calendar.
The Roman Martyrology describes the unnamed victims of this same persecution as 'the first fruits of the martyrs, which the Roman Church...
offered to God before the death of the Apostles' — that is, disciples of the Apostles themselves, martyred in this same wave of violence.

Unlike many early martyrs whose individual names and stories the Church has preserved, the ordinary Christians killed in Nero's persecution of 64 are remembered collectively, their identities lost to history even as the fact and manner of their deaths were recorded by a contemporary pagan historian with no reason to exaggerate Christian suffering.

This feast, added to the General Roman Calendar only in the 1969 reform, gives liturgical recognition to this vast, unnamed company of early Roman believers — a deliberate reminder, placed immediately after the solemnity of Peter and Paul, that the early Roman Church's foundation in blood was not the work of its most famous martyrs alone, but of countless ordinary Christians whose names are known only to God.
